skyline.text: How a helper sent up the road took the Vuelta
Ajay Shah’s case for knowing a sport without playing it
Why a whole doping era was struck from the record

footnote.text: I have no novel insights in this episode.

brief.head: Legs, not engines
brief.text: Unlike Formula One, road cycling pits one body against another on near-identical bikes, Amit Varma said. By a Grand Tour’s third week, it becomes “a test of pure character”. {053-C02}

brief.head: Orders from the car
brief.text: From the team car, a directeur sportif watching a TV feed radios instructions to the riders. Strategy is decided before a race, Amit Varma said; tactics during it. {053-C11}

brief.head: An hour, well lost
brief.text: Riders sharing a road may be playing different games. A sprinter after the green jersey’s points will happily lose an hour on a mountain stage, Amit Varma said. {053-C06}

brief.head: Small gains, big Sky
brief.text: Dave Brailsford’s Team Sky won seven Tours in eight years by chasing 1 per cent gains in diet, training, position and helmets, Amit Varma said. {053-C12}

brief.head: Luck of the wheel
brief.text: One touched wheel can bring down a whole group, Amit Varma said. Teams keep their leaders near the front of the peloton, but luck remains huge. {053-C14}

thought.text: You don’t have to be a hen to know about eggs.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, assuring Amit Varma that a fan who cannot ride may still understand cycling

lead.kicker: Amit Varma makes the case for cycling to Ajay Shah
lead.head: Chess in the slipstream
body: Amit Varma follows only three sports closely. One is chess. Cricket, he told Ajay Shah, is not one of the others. Another is cycling, and Shah wanted to know what there was in it.
A great deal, Varma argued. The sport demands much of the human body, spirit and character, and it “contains an element of chess”: months of preparation, and deep strategic and tactical thought.
He claimed no novelty. Nothing he would say, he warned, was unknown to people who follow cycling. He wanted to share a passion, with the episode timed for the start of the Tour de France.
Nor does he ride. His thought-to-action ratio for cycling, he told Shah, is zero: he never learned how. “Which I used to be very embarrassed about,” Varma said, “but now I’m like whatever.” {053-S02}
## How the sport sorts itself
Riders are sorted first by body weight, which they control only so far. Light riders climb better, and climbing, Varma said, is non-negotiable for anyone who wants to win a Grand Tour. {053-C04}

Heavier puncheurs bring explosive power to cobbles and short, steep hills. Sprinters save everything for the final stretch. Those who excel at none of these often become domestiques, working for the team’s stars.
What makes it a team sport is physics. A rider cuts through the air and leaves a pocket of low pressure behind him; the rider tucked into it saves about 30 per cent of his effort.
“All the people that you see on the screen who are cycling are not putting in equal effort,” Varma said. {053-C03}
Almost every tactic follows from that: domestiques shielding leaders, breakaways sharing turns in the wind, sprinters hiding until the last moment.
## A game of limited bullets
Early in a race, a few riders break clear of the main bunch, the peloton. Strangers share the work in silence, because a lone rider cannot stay away.
Near the finish, the cooperation collapses. All else being equal, the rider in front loses the sprint, so the leaders slow almost to a standstill, eyeing one another.

And every rider has only so many hard efforts in him. When one attacks, the others wait for someone else to chase. “Whoever spends energy chasing the first guy down will not have the energy to win in the end,” Varma said. “You have limited bullets.” {053-C09}
So two teammates can take turns attacking a lone rival until he is empty, and weaker riders can wear down a favourite without a word exchanged.
## Clean, and full of stories
The doping of the late 1990s and 2000s still shadows the sport. Varma argued that it is by and large clean today, because testing caught up and teams now police their own riders.
What keeps him watching is people. “We care about key rivalries, we care about redemption tales, and those matter a great deal,” he said. {053-C15}
Primož Roglič, the skier turned cyclist, still chasing the Tour. Tadej Pogačar against Jonas Vingegaard. Remco Evenepoel and Wout van Aert, two Belgians who sometimes share a national team.
Shah claimed childhood glory riding up a slope with both hands off. Had he been European, Varma suggested, cycling might have had him. “This is why economic development matters,” Shah replied.
Varma closed with a disclaimer: he is not an expert, just a passionate fan. His advice was simpler. “Go out and watch some cycling right now.”

second.label: Office cricket
second.head: Dravid retires hurt
second.deck: Amit Varma’s entire cricketing record: one wide, two wickets, one thrown bat
body: When Amit Varma was managing editor at Cricinfo, Rahul Dravid visited the office. The staff played a kind of office cricket with a ball halfway between a squeezy ball and a plastic ball. Spun forwards or backwards, it would zip through the air.
Varma persuaded Dravid to bat while he bowled. His first ball was a wide. Dravid was clean bowled by the next two. {053-S01}

Dravid called him Shoaib Akhtar, refused to play on and threw the bat away. That, Varma said, is the sum of his action in cricket. “You would not actually see me on a cricket field running around and doing things,” he said. “I’m Bengali.” {#bengali}

quote.text: My first ball was a wide. Didn’t work out. He was clean bowled off the next two balls.

second.caption: bowling Rahul Dravid

third.head: Beaten by another planet
body: In the Covid year, 2020, Primož Roglič led the Tour de France into its second-last stage, a time trial. His 21-year-old compatriot Tadej Pogačar sat about 30 seconds behind.
Starting last, Roglič heard on the radio that Pogačar had caught his time, then passed it. On the final climb, Amit Varma said, you could almost see tears in his eyes. {053-S12}
People called it a collapse. Varma calls that narrative false. “Roglič came fifth in the stage out of hundred and fifty people,” he said. {#fifth} Pogačar was simply on another planet.
Afterwards the 30-year-old Roglič found Pogačar, shook his hand and hugged him. Varma, watching live, had tweeted that it was one of the seminal moments in world sport.

p2.title: Reading the race
p2.deck: How road cycling works, from kinds of races to the doping years, as Amit Varma explained it

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: No bike, no problem
sections.caption: watching a sport he cannot ride
body: Ajay Shah opened with a jab: Amit Varma, he said, looked like a guy who would be very fast on a cycle. The Bengali in Varma did not appreciate the low blow. {053-J01}

Shah then rated his co-host’s “thought to action ratio” in each of his sports. Poker is high: Varma played professionally for a few years. In chess, Shah said, he has had the heart-stopping moments at the board.
Cycling is zero. Varma never learned to ride. His father was in the IAS and there was always a car, and his working life in Bombay ran on local trains and buses until he bought one. {053-S02}
He is now, he claimed, the best driver in Bombay, “because driving in Bombay is not about driving, it is about Bombay”. {053-J02}
## Hens and eggs

So everything Varma knows about cycling is purely intellectual, built from watching a lot of it. Shah supplied the licence. “You don’t have to be a hen to know about eggs,” he said. “In fact, being a hen is an impediment to knowing about eggs.” {053-C01}
Then he christened the hour: “Welcome to a scrambled eggs episode on cycling.” {053-J03}
~ It was, Shah noted at the start, another of the pair’s off-beat episodes, after those on chess, hiking and Bruce Springsteen.

quote.text: And in cycles, it is literally zero because I don’t know how to ride a cycle.

sections.label: The races
sections.head: Monuments, tours and a clock
sections.caption: the kinds of races
body: Amit Varma started from the basics, and with road cycling only, not the indoor events of the Olympics.

The simplest race runs a single day from one point to another, five to seven hours in the saddle. Many prestigious races of this kind are called classics, and five of them are the monuments: Milan-San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and the Giro di Lombardia. {#monuments}

Their terrain differs. Liège and Lombardia are hilly. Flanders and Roubaix are flat but cobbled, which demands explosive power. Milan-San Remo is flat until hills near the end, and anybody can win it.
## Against the clock
A time trial is one man against the clock. {#clock} Riders set off a minute or two apart, and one who catches another may not ride in his slipstream.
Then there are the stage races: about seven important one-week races, and three Grand Tours, in Italy, France and Spain, of three weeks each. {#grandtours}
These mix flat, hilly and mountain stages. A summit finish such as Alpe d’Huez, Varma said, sorts out the climbers. {053-J13}

~ Winning a Grand Tour, above all the Tour de France, is the great prize. Varma discovered cycling watching the Tour in the late 1990s, before he understood its tactics, and saw at once the scale of the endurance.

quote.text: That really separates the great climbers from the not so great climbers.

sections.label: The riders
sections.head: You are what you weigh
sections.caption: who climbs and who sprints
body: Cycling mixes nature and nurture, Amit Varma said, but it is a lot about nature, above all body weight, which a rider can control only up to a point.

On long mountains a heavier rider must spend more watts to cover the same ground. So today’s Grand Tour stars, Pogačar, Vingegaard, Roglič and Evenepoel, are all light, between about 61 and 65 kilos. {053-C04}
The heaviest top riders are in the late 70s: Wout van Aert is 78 kg, Mathieu van der Poel 75. {#weights}
They are puncheurs, spelt the French way: too heavy for long climbs but explosive on flats, cobbles and short, steep hills, which suits them to the one-day classics. {#puncheurs}
## Many races on one road
Sprinters do nothing all stage, sheltered by their teams, and save everything for a burst over the last 30 to 70 metres.
Grand Tours hand out several prizes: overall time, the Tour’s yellow jersey; points, its green; and mountain points. {#yellow}
Riders who excel at none of these often become domestiques, a French term for those whose job is to help the team’s stars. {#domestique}
~ Weight is not quite everything. The world time trial champion, Remco Evenepoel, is a GC rider of 61 kg, Varma said, and “just fantastic”.

quote.text: If you are a lighter rider, you are likely to be a better climber.

sections.label: The physics
sections.head: Thirty per cent off
sections.caption: why cycling is a team sport
body: Ajay Shah could see the pieces but not how they fit together. How, he asked, does cycling become a team sport?
Through physics, Amit Varma said, invoking his co-host’s standing as a card-carrying physicist and aeronautical engineer. {053-J04}
A cycle cutting through the air leaves a pocket of low pressure behind it, almost a vacuum. A rider in that pocket escapes the wind. “I can save 30% of my effort,” Varma said. {#thirty}
## Seven Amits and an Ajay
He made it concrete. Imagine Shah as the star sprinter on a flat stage, with seven Amits on the team to protect him. {#amits}
Each Amit rides in front, taking the wind, until he is spent. Then he drifts aside to finish at his own pace, and the next Amit takes over, until Shah is delivered to the end.

Nobody improvises alone. Every team is miked up, and a directeur sportif follows in a car with the television feed. The terms are French because the French were the pioneers of European cycling. {#french}
~ Shah had read that basketball coaches watch their players’ live data and pull tired ones out. {#basketball} Cycling has the data, Varma said, but no rider can be swapped mid-race.

quote.text: It is the guys who are out on the wind who are putting in that effort, and the people behind them are not.

sections.label: The tactics
sections.head: Cooperate now, betray later
sections.caption: the game theory of the breakaway
body: Strangers in a breakaway share the work without a word, each taking a turn in the wind. Sitting in without working, Amit Varma said, is “desperately uncool”, unless your team leader is chasing behind. {053-C08}
The peloton has an edge. A breakaway rider must ration himself for 100 kilometres; a domestique at the front of the bunch is told to empty himself over 20. {053-C07}
So the chasing teams hold the gap at about three minutes and time the catch for the closing kilometres. Catch it too early, and another breakaway forms.
## The Sky Train

A strong team can smother a whole race. US Postal under Lance Armstrong, and later Team Sky for Chris Froome, set a pace on the flat that no one could attack from, then sent mountain domestiques to the front one by one. {053-C10}
The peloton stretched into a single line. Rivals lost their helpers; the leader kept his.
Food is tactics too. A rider who runs out of calories has “bonked”, so the team car reminds riders to eat and domestiques ferry bars and drinks forward. {#bonk}
~ Are there pacts between teams before a race? None, Varma told Ajay Shah. Within a team, everyone knows his role, but the role is dynamic.

quote.text: Beyond a certain pace, no one can jump away from you. The acceleration and power required is too much.

sections.label: The dark age
sections.head: The decade that didn’t count
sections.caption: doping and the clean-up
body: Ajay Shah raised the doping question. In the Olympics, he said, it seems like an arms race where testing is always trying to keep up. {#armsrace}

Cycling had one too, Amit Varma said. He recalled that Greg LeMond, or perhaps another top rider, took a few months off around the late 1980s and came back to find he could barely keep up with the peloton. {053-S13}
Through the 1990s everyone was on drugs, Varma said, with EPO giving effects like those of altitude training. From 1996, the Tour’s winners for a decade or more were all doping. {#tainted}

Which is why, Varma said, it is shady to single out one villain. The authorities did not promote the runners-up; they declared that a whole period’s results, all seven of Lance Armstrong’s wins included, do not count.
## Watch in good faith
The arms race ran to the start of the 2010s. Then testing caught up with the cheats, and teams, which suffer when a rider is caught, began policing their own. {053-C13}
Today’s speeds, Varma argued, come from better training, such as weeks at altitude. Fans can watch in good faith.
~ Wout van Aert skipped this year’s cyclocross world championship to prepare at altitude for the cobbled classics, then crashed at the Tour of Flanders through no fault of his own. {053-S14}

quote.text: They could barely keep up with the peloton because the pace was so incredibly high and they realized something is fishy.

side.boxText: Amit Varma’s viewing guide: Chris Horner, the oldest man to win a Grand Tour, who reviews each day’s racing and calls wasteful teams “knuckleheads”; and the *Lanterne Rouge Cycling Podcast*, whose Patrick and Benji do hour-long deep dives. {053-R04}

contQuote.text: We follow sport not just to see the limits of human achievement, but we get caught up in the stories of the people who are involved.

p3.title: Stories from the road
p3.deck: Decoys, stalemates and accidents: the races Amit Varma retells, and what they teach

stories.start: last year's Vuelta Hispana, which is the last of the three week grand tours
stories.end: I want always to be the leader of the team when I am racing
stories.caption: Sepp Kuss’s Vuelta
stories.kicker: How Jumbo-Visma’s plan for the Vuelta worked too well
stories.head: The domestique who kept the jersey
body: Jumbo-Visma, then the strongest team, came to the 2023 Vuelta a España with two leaders. Primož Roglič had won that year’s Giro d’Italia and the previous three Vueltas. Jonas Vingegaard had just won the Tour de France.
They also had Sepp Kuss, in Amit Varma’s telling one of the world’s best mountain domestiques, a support rider who had helped Roglič win the Giro and Vingegaard the Tour.

The rival was Remco Evenepoel of Quick-Step, and the plan was clever. Send Kuss up the road in a breakaway and into the leader’s red jersey, so that Evenepoel’s team would wear itself out chasing a helper. When Evenepoel was spent, Roglič or Vingegaard would attack.

The plan worked too well. Evenepoel simply collapsed, lost a few minutes and was out of the race. Kuss led, with Roglič second and Vingegaard third. The team had the top three places, and someone had to win.

Roglič, ambitious and long unlucky at the Tour de France, wanted to race for it. He had come there to win, he said, and should be allowed to beat his teammate. Then came outrage on social media: for years Kuss had helped them win, and here was a chance, Varma said, to “gift him something beautiful”. {053-S06}
Vingegaard, having just won the Tour, was cool with that. So Jumbo-Visma let Kuss win, and its riders finished one, two, three. {#podium}
~ Roglič was furious. He left for another team, Bora-Hansgrohe, Varma said, wanting always to be his team’s leader when he races.
stories.why: Team roles are fixed in theory but dynamic in practice. When a plan succeeds beyond its design, loyalty, ambition and public feeling collide, and the result can cost a team its leader.
stories.postscript: Lance Armstrong once told his domestique Floyd Landis to “run like you stole something”. When rivals held Landis, Armstrong won the stage himself. {053-S07}

stories.start: a truly great race was the tour of Flanders in 2022
stories.end: sprinter of the bunch. So it didn't kind of work out for him
stories.caption: Pogačar’s stalemate at Flanders
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the 2022 Tour of Flanders
stories.head: Cat, mouse and three chasers
body: At the 2022 Tour of Flanders, Tadej Pogačar, 65 kg and a superb climber, attacked on the hills. Only Mathieu van der Poel, 75 kg, a lesser climber but a far better sprinter, could stay with him, Amit Varma said.

On the flat run-in, Pogačar knew he could only beat Van der Poel by coming out of his slipstream. {#pogslip} So he refused to lead. Both slowed almost to a standstill, eyeing each other, while three riders behind, with nothing to lose, cooperated flat out to catch them.
They did. Van der Poel won the sprint, Dylan van Baarle was second and Valentin Madouas third. Pogačar, the dominant rider all day, was fourth.
~ That, Varma said, was “because he waited too long and the other guys caught up and then he’s the worst sprinter of the bunch”. {053-S04}
stories.why: Cat-and-mouse games have a hidden cost. While two rivals optimise against each other, riders nobody is watching can close the gap, and the cleverest move of the day becomes self-defeating.

stories.start: the only time this backfired, I think, was a 2005 or 2004
stories.end: And after Floyd got disqualified, he became Tour de France champion
stories.caption: Oscar Pereiro’s lucky Tour
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Tour de France won by being ignored
stories.head: Overlooked, then crowned
body: Contenders in a Grand Tour often let a harmless breakaway go, Amit Varma said, sure that they can catch anyone who matters. The one time he recalls it backfiring was a Tour de France of 2005 or 2004; he forgot which year. The breakaway carried Oscar Pereiro, not a great climber and not seen as a contender.

He gained enough time to lead the race for a while, and nobody much cared. The real fight was behind him, against the eventual winner, Floyd Landis, if Varma remembered rightly. “All the other contenders were fighting with Floyd, so they completely ignored this guy,” Varma said. Pereiro finished second. {053-S03}
Then Landis was disqualified for drug use, and Pereiro became Tour de France champion.
~ He was, Varma said, one of two lucky beneficiaries; the other won last year’s Vuelta. {#lucky}
stories.why: Letting a harmless rider go is a calculated risk. When every rival watches one threat, the man nobody is watching can walk off with the prize, and luck can finish the job.

stories.start: I want to tell you a story about a skiing accident which happened
stories.end: And he becomes one of the great riders of his generation
stories.caption: Roglič’s skiing crash
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Primož Roglič’s second sporting life
stories.head: From the piste to the peloton
body: Around 2007 or 2008, at a junior world championship, a teenager from Slovenia had a terrible skiing crash. Amit Varma still goes back to the footage once in a while. You worry, he said, whether he will walk again.
He was Primož Roglič. He did ski again, but realised he would not be among the world’s best, perhaps because the injury cost him a developmental phase, perhaps for mental reasons.
“I love sport, man. I just love sport,” Varma recalled him saying. “I want to go out there, I want to compete, I want to be physical.” So he took up cycling. {053-S11}

~ He came to it relatively late, which is why some say he is not a great bike handler. He became one of the great riders of his generation anyway, and won the Vuelta a España three times. {#threevueltas}
stories.why: A forced change of course, made late, can still lead to greatness when the drive behind it is intact. Roglič’s redemption story, Varma said, has still not fully played out.
stories.postscript: In the weeks before this year’s Tour, he crashed alongside Vingegaard and Evenepoel at the Tour of the Basque Country.

quiz.q: How much effort, by Amit Varma’s account, does a rider save in another’s slipstream?
quiz.a: About 30 per cent, since the rider in front takes all the wind.

quiz.q: Why did Tadej Pogačar, the day’s strongest rider, finish only fourth at the 2022 Tour of Flanders?
quiz.a: He stalled to stay in Van der Poel’s slipstream, and three chasers caught up.

quiz.q: What did Dave Brailsford call his method of finding 1 per cent improvements everywhere?
quiz.a: The aggregation of marginal gains, which took Team Sky to seven Tour wins.

quiz.q: Who became Tour de France champion after Floyd Landis was disqualified for drug use?
quiz.a: Oscar Pereiro, a breakaway rider the other contenders had completely ignored.

quiz.q: What did Lance Armstrong tell his domestique Floyd Landis near the top of the final mountain?
quiz.a: “Run like you stole something”, because he wanted Landis to win the stage.

quiz.q: What is Amit Varma’s “thought to action ratio” in cycling, and why?
quiz.a: Literally zero, because he has never learned how to ride a cycle.
